response.overallSummary: Simulated choices for the printed San Leandro BT11 ballot of November 3, 2026, using official proposition pages, the state certified-candidate list, and reporting available through October 27, 2026. Preferences favor accessible elections, targeted public goods, and fiscal designs that can be administered; they reject voter-ID ballot invalidation, minority vetoes of local taxes, and poorly targeted or rigid fiscal mandates. Thin comparative records produced abstentions rather than invented rankings.

The $11.25 billion bond is aimed at veterans, supportive, and affordable housing with stated oversight, matching a documented shortage better than leaving that pipeline unfunded.
Raising budget reserves and extending extra debt payments is sound insurance against California’s volatile revenues, despite a real concern that reserve deposits could affect spending-limit rebates.
Extending the existing tax on incomes above about $371,000 avoids a 2031 schools-and-healthcare cliff without a new middle-income tax, though it deepens reliance on volatile high-earner revenue.
Letting governments offer optional public campaign financing, while barring education, transportation, and safety funds, improves participation without mandating a blank check.
Separating recall from replacement stops a successor from winning with a small plurality and returns vacancies to special election or ordinary appointment.
A $25 billion program covering up to 17 percent of new homes priced near $1.5 million is weakly targeted and more likely to subsidize new-home demand than the households with the greatest need.
An $8.4 billion general-obligation bond that sends half the proceeds to one UC-affiliated institute creates decades of debt and is less flexible than competitive research budgeting.

Invalidating mail ballots that omit ID digits and blocking in-person voting without government ID would cost tens to hundreds of millions and burden eligible voters beyond existing signature verification.

A one-time 5 percent billionaire tax could raise substantial health revenue, but residency dating to January 1, 2026, hard-to-value assets, and exemption from school-funding and spending limits make this design a poor constitutional instrument.
Required audits are separable from the measure’s broader ban on new state taxes that sit outside the spending limit, which would constrain future revenue choices.
Barring every new state tax on personal property, and nullifying conflicting taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, is a sweeping constitutional lock rather than a fix for one flawed proposal.
Raising the threshold for voter-proposed local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds lets a minority block fire, school, and infrastructure funding.
A rigid 90 percent program-spending penalty can treat necessary facilities and administration as violations and risks closing clinics that serve underserved patients.
Deadlines could speed housing, but the measure also covers most transportation, water, and health projects and narrows what courts may review, which is broader than a targeted housing fix.
A temporary half-cent sales tax with stated oversight is a regressive but practical way to avoid major BART and regional transit cuts and the resulting congestion.

Renewing the expiring $99 parcel tax for twelve years, with senior and disability exemptions, a separate account, audit, and citizen oversight, is a modest and accountable school-funding continuation.

compass.explanation: Economic −4 reflects Yes votes for targeted housing bonds, the high-income school-and-health tax, transit, and the school parcel tax (ca-proposition-1, ca-proposition-3, alameda-measure-rtm, alameda-measure-j) and No votes against constitutional tax bans and a minority local-tax veto (ca-proposition-41, ca-proposition-42, ca-proposition-43), offset by rejecting a flawed wealth tax, a concentrated research bond, a middle-income mortgage subsidy, a rigid clinic ratio, and broad CEQA rollback while supporting larger reserves (ca-proposition-40, ca-proposition-38, ca-proposition-37, ca-proposition-44, ca-proposition-45, ca-proposition-2). Social −6 reflects opposition to ID-based ballot invalidation, support for optional public campaign finance and a majority-respecting recall fix, retention of judges absent unfitness, and candidate choices favoring inclusive schools and limits on encampment and immigration coercion (ca-proposition-39, ca-proposition-4, ca-proposition-5, retention-kelli-m-evans, state-superintendent-of-public-instruction, governor). Tension: No on ca-proposition-40 is a design judgment, not opposition to taxing extreme wealth; No on ca-proposition-45 preserves regulation while for-mayor-san-leandro and governor still favor more housing supply. Abstentions were not scored as centrist zeros.

limitations: The November 3, 2026 date and proposition titles were verified on the Secretary of State guide; this is not a prior cycle’s similarly numbered ballot.
The full 965-page county guide and complete state voter-guide PDF were not read page by page; official proposition pages, the certified list, and search excerpts were used.
No material inventory error was found. Appellate retention names were not rechecked one by one against the PDF in this session, and votes were not based on opinion-level review.
Several contests were abstained because challenger or multi-candidate records were not retrieved; incumbency alone was not treated as a full policy comparison.
San Leandro candidate statements and the Maes platform are campaign statements, not independent outcome findings.
Measure RTM was judged from the county question text, not the full measure PDF.
The printed BT11 sample includes multiple San Leandro council districts; choices follow that printed inventory and are not personal voting advice.
Sources were consulted on or before the October 27, 2026 Pacific cutoff; no election results were used.
